name: Aharhel
title: Descendant of Judah mentioned in the genealogies of Chronicles
summary: Aharhel appears exclusively in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles (4:8). He is mentioned alongside Anub in a genealogical note connected to Kos, but the Hebrew syntax of the verse is difficult to interpret, and there is uncertainty regarding the exact family relationships—including who was father to whom. Harum is mentioned in this context and understood in several interpretations as his father. Beyond this genealogical information, there are no biblical narratives about Aharhel's life or deeds. Nevertheless, his inclusion in Judah's tribal register testifies that his lineage was counted among the recognized families of the tribe. Such lists held great practical and identity-forming significance, especially in the period after the Babylonian exile when the books of Chronicles took their final form.
roles: Member of the tribe of Judah

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Judah's family tree
keyEvents.description: Aharhel is mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles, within a genealogical sequence linked to Koz. Along with Anub, he represents a branch of Judah's descendants.

keyEvents.title: Genealogical context: Koz and his descendants
keyEvents.description: Aharhel appears in a genealogical sequence where Koz is named as the ancestor of several individuals. The syntax of the Hebrew text makes it challenging to determine the exact family relationships, but he clearly belongs to this lineage within the tribe of Judah.

versions.summary: Aharhel is a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. He was the son of Harum and belonged to the descendants of Koz. He is known only from a brief genealogical reference, and there are no further biblical accounts of his life or deeds.
versions.title: Descendant of Judah
versions.reason: [major] Aharhel is mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 4, which cover the lineage of the tribe of Judah. Although his exact lifespan is unknown, he is typically placed in the period after the patriarchs. The genealogies in Chronicles span a broad era, but the context suggests he lived later, likely during the time of the judges or the united monarchy. 'patriarchs' is misleading since the patriarchal age usually refers to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.; [major] Calling Aharhel a 'patriarch' is misleading. He is a genealogical figure mentioned in a family tree, not a patriarch in the biblical sense (such as Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob). A more fitting role would be 'ancestor' or 'head of a clan' within the tribe of Judah.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could clarify that Aharhel belongs to the descendants of Kos according to the context in 1 Chron 4:7-8. His relationship to Kos should be made clearer.; [minor] The fourth key event ('The significance of the tribe in Israel's history') is very general and concerns more the tribe of Judah as a whole than Aharhel specifically. It is not an event connected to Aharhel and should either be removed or rephrased.; [minor] The relationship between Aharhel and Kos: In 1 Chron 4:7-8, Kos is mentioned as the father of Anub and Hasobeba and of Aharhel's clans, while Harum is named as the father of Aharhel. This connection should be described more accurately to avoid confusion.; [minor] There are no footnotes covering linguistic, historical, or theological details about Aharhel, such as the meaning of his name in Hebrew or the context of the genealogies in Chronicles.

He is known only from a brief genealogical reference in 1 Chronicles 4:8, and there are no further biblical accounts of his life or deeds. His inclusion in the genealogy testifies that his family held an acknowledged place within the tribe of Judah.
versions.title: Descendant of Judah mentioned in the genealogies
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 in its phrasing. It should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from earlier versions. Additionally, the claim that Aharhel belongs to the 'descendants of Kos' is based on a specific reading of the context in 1 Chr 4:8; the text directly states that Kos fathered Anub and Aharhel (depending on translation), but the connection between Kos and Harum remains unclear. This should be formulated more cautiously.; [minor] The phrasing 'His inclusion in the genealogy testifies that his family held an acknowledged place within the tribe of Judah' is a reasonable interpretation, but it could be strengthened by placing it in the context of the function of genealogies after the exile.; [minor] The era 'judges' is uncertain. We do not actually know when Aharhel lived—the genealogies in 1 Chronicles place him among Judah's descendants, but the exact time period is unknown. 'Judges' is an acceptable assumption, though 'patriarchs' or 'united kingdom' could also be argued. It is retained as is, but this uncertainty should be noted.; [minor] The third key event element ('genealogy of the tribe of Judah') is very general and adds little specific information about Aharhel. Consider removing it or replacing it with something more precise.; [minor] In 1 Chr 4:8, the text can be read as indicating that Kos was the father of Anub and Aharhel, while Harum is connected to another part of the passage. The relationship between Harum and Aharhel as father and son depends on how one reads the Hebrew text. Some readings place Harum as the father, others see Kos as the father. The profile should be clearer about this uncertainty.; [minor] The footnotes are good, but the third footnote concerning the priestly family of Kos in Ezra 2:61/Neh 7:63 refers to Hakkoz (הַקּוֹץ), who may possibly be a different person or lineage. It should be clarified that this connection is uncertain.

versions.summary: Aharhel is a figure who appears in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles. He is mentioned in connection with Kos and Harum in 1 Chronicles 4:8, but the exact familial relationship between these individuals is debated due to the complex Hebrew syntax of the verse. Aharhel is known exclusively from this genealogical note, and no biblical narratives describe his life or work. Nevertheless, his inclusion in Judah's family register suggests that his family was counted among the recognized clans of the tribe – something that had practical significance in the post-exilic period when these lists were compiled and recorded.
versions.title: Descendant of Judah mentioned in the genealogies
versions.reason: [major] Aharhel is known exclusively from the genealogies in 1 Chronicles 1–9, which were compiled during the Persian period after the exile. We have no information that places him specifically in the time of the judges. The eras 'patriarchs' or 'divided-kingdom' are also uncertain. Given that the genealogies in 1 Chronicles typically cover periods from the patriarchs onward, and that many of the obscure names in the Judah lists likely belong to the period before or during the monarchy, 'united-kingdom' or 'divided-kingdom' are more probable than 'judges'. But since we truly do not know, it is most honest to choose a broad category. Among the available options, 'divided-kingdom' is a reasonable choice because many of the family names in 1 Chr 4 likely originate from this period.; [minor] The role 'patriarch of the tribe of Judah' is acceptable, but it can be debated whether we should call him a patriarch without knowing if he had descendants. A more neutral role such as 'member of the tribe of Judah' or 'clan leader in the tribe of Judah' may be more precise.; [minor] The father is given as 'Harum', but 1 Chr 4:8 is syntactically ambiguous. Some interpretations see Kos as the father of Anub and Aharhel, not Harum. Since the text is disputed, this should be reflected better. Nevertheless, Harum is a common interpretation, so it can be retained with a caveat.; [minor] The second key event actually concerns the same verse and context as the first. For a person mentioned in only one verse, it may be considered whether two events are necessary. The event is still informative and provides useful context.; [minor] The last footnote is categorized as 'theological', but the content deals primarily with textual criticism and syntactic analysis of the Hebrew text, which is more linguistic than theological.

footnotes.text: The name Aharhel (Hebrew: אַחַרְחֵל, 'Aḥarḥēl') appears only in 1 Chron. 4:8 and is a hapax legomenon in the Hebrew Bible. Its etymology is debated; possible interpretations include "behind the fortification" or a combination of elements that may mean "after" and "fear/pain." The exact meaning remains uncertain.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 1–9 were likely edited and compiled during the Persian period, after the return from the Babylonian exile. They served as a basis for restoring tribal identity, inheritance rights, and connections to lands in Judah.

Kos (Hebrew: קוֹץ) is mentioned in 1 Chron. 4:8 in connection with several families of Judah. The name may mean "thorn." A priestly family called Hakkoz (הַקּוֹץ) is mentioned in Ezra 2:61 and Neh. 7:63, but it is uncertain whether there is any connection between them.

The Hebrew text of 1 Chron. 4:8 is syntactically complex, and scholars disagree on how to understand the family relationships among Kos, Harum, Anub, and Aharhel. Hebrew uses the expression "holid" (הוֹלִיד, "begot"), but it is unclear who is the subject and object in the verse, leading to various possible reconstructions of the family tree.

Rabbinic tradition has generally not paid much attention to Aharhel, but some midrashic commentaries on Chronicles attempt to link obscure names in the genealogies with well-known biblical figures or to derive moral lessons from the meanings of the names.
